subject: ggplot does not respect pointsize of the graphic device

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: ggplot does not respect pointsize of the graphic device
parts:
Hi all,

I was annoyed by how large the text on ggplots was when the device
window is small (on my laptop). It appaers changing the pointsize does
not affect the text. It seems to affect margins a bit but that's all.

library("ggplot2")

# on OS X
quartz.options(pointsize=9)
quartz()
plot(0)
quartz()
qplot(0,0)

quartz.options(pointsize=2)
quartz()
plot(0)
quartz()
qplot(0,0)

quartz.options(pointsize=20)
quartz()
plot(0)
quartz()
qplot(0,0)


# on linux (and OS X)
X11.options(pointsize=9)
X11()
plot(0)
X11()
qplot(0,0)

X11.options(pointsize=2)
X11()
plot(0)
X11()
qplot(0,0)

X11.options(pointsize=20)
X11()
plot(0)
X11()
qplot(0,0)


Thanks in advance for help/workarounds.

JiHO

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Theming, was Re: ggplot does not respect pointsize of the graphic device
parts:
> I was annoyed by how large the text on ggplots was when the device
> window is small (on my laptop). It appaers changing the pointsize
> does not affect the text. It seems to affect margins a bit but
> that's all.

So I was about to reply to my own question (... once again. Sorry
everyone, I really need to look harder before resorting to ask the
list) when Hadley gave the solution I also found in the book:
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size=9))

Yet, not respecting the pointsize of the device might still be
considered as a bug by some. Especially since there is a complex
interaction between base_size in ggplot and pointsize on the device.
As a rule of thumb, I found that pointsize and base_size must be equal
for ggplots to look harmonious (i.e. as in the book / as Hadley
supposedly designed them to be).

Example (to be run on OS X, but just replace quartz() by X11() on
linux and the result is the same)

library(ggplot2)

p = qplot(runif(5),runif(5)) + opts(title="A dumb plot")

# this is the default
theme_set(theme_grey(12))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=12)
p

# this has display issues (overwriting in legends etc.) because the
font size is too large compared to what the device "expects"
theme_set(theme_grey(25))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=8)
p

# when the pointsize is set accordingly, the proportions are
"harmonious" again (well, it still does not look great that's because
25 is much to big for this size of plot)
theme_set(theme_grey(25))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=25)
p

# Ahhh, that's better
theme_set(theme_grey(10))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=10)
p


Beyond this issue, I took this opportunity to try and fix some old
theming code I had. It is too bad that (for consistency and robustness
purposes I guess) the theming has had to become so complicated. Before
I could do:

foo <- list(grid.fill="white", grid.minour.colour="black")
.
.
.
ggtheme(foo)

an ggplot would modify *only* those two elements in the theme current
when ggtheme is called (which can be different fro; the one foo was
defined in) and keep the defaults for the rest. Now I must write:

theme_update(panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white"),
panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour = "black"))

which is significantly more convoluted but, more importantly does not
seem to be "storable" as easily. The only way I found to "store" the
modifications of a few theme properties was:

# store the current theme for reference
old = theme_get()
# go back to default
theme_set(theme_gray())
# do some modifs
theme_update(panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white"),
panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour = "black"))
# store the full theme: default + modifs in a variable
foo = theme_get()
# go back to state before doing all that
theme_set(old)
.
.
.
# somewhere else, use the modifications in foo
theme_set(foo)

Which kind of works, even though the appearance induced by foo now
depends on the environment in which theme_update was initially called
(i.e. the default gray here) not the one in which theme_set(foo) is
called later. But that might be for the best: it is more reliable/
predictable.
Yet it seems convoluted. Is there any easier way I missed?

JiHO
